title: The City’s price per home against buildings that changed hands nearby
question: How does the price the public paid per home compare with the value per unit that recent sales set on multi-unit buildings in the same neighbourhood?
finding: 11 purchases of finished residential buildings have a known number of homes. For 11 of them at least three multi-unit buildings show a sale date in the two years before (10 within the same neighbourhood, the rest only citywide). The public price per home was 0.4 to 2.2 times the middle value per unit those sales set; 2 were at 1.5 times or more, led by 333-12th Street at $852,941 a home against $392,854 (40 sales). Against every multi-unit building in the neighbourhood, sold or not, the price per home runs from 0.6 to 5.4 times the middle assessed value per unit, which mostly measures how long the neighbours have been held.
how: Price per home is the purchase price over the homes counted in the property screens: the State’s Homekey award list where it covers the building, otherwise the Budget Analyst’s 2024 audit or the assessor roll; the “Homes counted from” column says which, and gives the audit’s count where the two differ. Comparable sales are buildings of five or more units, hotels and residential hotels on the full 2019, 2022 and 2025 rolls whose sale date falls in the two years before the public purchase, valued per unit (per room where the roll gives no units) on the first of those rolls after the sale; the same class in the same neighbourhood is used where at least three exist, then all multi-unit buildings in the neighbourhood, then the same class citywide, and the count is shown. The second comparison is the middle assessed value per unit of every such building in the neighbourhood on the roll before the purchase, from the neighbourhood table, with the number of parcels behind it and the number the roll records as sold that year or the year before.
limits: The roll records no price. The value that appears after a sale date is an indicator of the price, because California law re-sets assessed value to the price paid when a property changes hands; exemptions, a transfer of part of a property, transfers the law excludes from reassessment and new construction all break that link. The recorded deed and its transfer-tax declaration at the Assessor-Recorder would settle what was paid; neither is open data. The neighbourhood table on disk gives the middle value of all buildings, not of those that sold, so the sold comparison was rebuilt from the three full rolls on disk and is thin: sale dates are sparse on the rolls from 2020 on, and some comparisons rest on three to five sales. Buildings differ in age, condition, unit size and whether a unit is a room or a flat; a new apartment block bought complete will sit far above the middle of an old neighbourhood for that reason alone. The all-buildings comparison is context, not a measure of overpayment: long-held buildings are assessed far below what they would sell for.
